# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy v2
*Drafted 16 November 2026. Supersedes everything in `old/`.*

## Mission

Contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

## Honest assessment of our position

One founder with evenings and weekends, good writing, okay Python, up to $2,000
of personal funds this year, at least one skilled volunteer (data analyst,
~5 hrs/week), and — until an HR conversation at Morgan's employer happens —
no ability to put Morgan's name on anything public.

This rules out: original frontier research, anything requiring full-time
attention, anything requiring immediate public advocacy. It does **not** rule
out careful, durable, verifiable work that compounds.

## The chosen wedge: the Threshold Tracker

**A public, maintained ledger of concrete safety commitments made by frontier
AI developers and governments — and whether they are being kept.**

Examples of what it tracks:
- Lab safety frameworks / responsible scaling policies: the specific capability
  thresholds, evaluation triggers, and deployment conditions they promise.
- Government and summit pledges (e.g. incident reporting, pre-deployment
  testing access, compute-threshold notifications).
- Status over time: kept / modified / quietly weakened / abandoned, each with
  citations to primary sources.

### Why this, out of the four candidate ideas

1. **Neglected.** Commentary on AI safety is abundant; patient, sourced
   accountability for what was actually promised is scarce. Promises are made
   at summit cadence and forgotten at news cadence.
2. **Leverage without authority.** Nobody needs to know who we are for a
   well-sourced table to be useful. Journalists, researchers, grantmakers and
   policy staff can all cite it. Credibility comes from citations, not from
   Morgan's résumé.
3. **Fits our actual capacity.** Writing-heavy, steady-effort, parallelizable
   with volunteers. A data analyst with 5 hrs/week is almost exactly the
   right first collaborator.
4. **Robust to worldview.** Useful whether you expect doom or transformation:
   a world where commitments are tracked and kept is better along nearly every
   path to superintelligence.
5. **Compatible with the name-constraint.** All pre-launch work (schema,
   data collection, verification) is private. We launch publicly only after
   HR clearance.

### Rejected alternatives (for now, with reasons)

- **Newsletter** — crowded; Morgan's own note says so. Revisit only as a
  changelog for the tracker.
- **Reading group** — nice, low leverage, doesn't compound.
- **Small-grants fund** — $2k is too little to regrant meaningfully; better to
  *receive* a grant (Emberfall) than to give tiny ones.
- **Original evals** — "evals for something nobody is measuring" is the same
  instinct as the tracker (measure the unmeasured), but policy/commitment
  tracking needs no compute, no model access, and no ML depth we don't have.

## Phases

**Phase 0 — private groundwork (now → HR clearance)**
- Build the schema and seed ~30 verified commitment entries (`tracker/`).
- Onboard Priya Raman on data collection and verification protocol.
- Submit Emberfall rapid-grant application (Morgan as named applicant,
  deadline 30 Nov) — see `proposals/`.
- Morgan files Dorrance outside-activities disclosure (due 30 Nov) and has
  the HR conversation. **This is the critical path to everything public.**

**Phase 1 — quiet launch (after HR clearance)**
- Publish site + tracker at halcyonthreshold.org (Pagewell free tier is fine).
- File the FMIR-2026-0042-style comments in future dockets under Morgan's name.
- Write one launch post for Alignment Commons (they have an open call).
- Share with the meetup network and the Safety Ledger.

**Phase 2 — cadence (if Phase 1 gets any traction)**
- Monthly "commitment delta" report: what changed this month.
- Recruit 2–3 more volunteer verifiers; two-person rule on every status change.

## Principles

- **Primary sources only; every claim cited; corrections published.** The
  entire value of this project is that it is boring and right.
- **No alarmism, no boosterism.** We report what was promised and what
  happened. Readers draw conclusions.
- **Honesty about scale.** We are small. We never imply otherwise.
- **Hard lines:** stay under budget cap; nothing public before HR clearance;
  no unsolicited-invoice payments (see `ops/decision-log.md` — scam attempt
  already received).

## Metrics that would tell us it's working (check March 2027)

- Tracker cited by ≥3 independent parties (article, paper, or policy doc).
- ≥50 verified entries, each with a primary source.
- External funding secured so Morgan's personal spend stays ≤ $2,000.
- If none of these by March: write a post-mortem and pick a new wedge.

# Threshold Tracker — working data

**Status: pre-launch. Nothing here is published or verified to publication standard yet.**

## What an entry is

One entry = one concrete, checkable commitment by a frontier AI developer or a
government, e.g. "Lab X's safety framework commits to running evaluation suite
Y before deploying models above capability threshold Z."

Vague aspirations ("we take safety seriously") are not entries. If it can't be
checked, it isn't tracked.

## Schema (`commitments.csv`)

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| id | stable id, e.g. HT-0001 |
| actor | who made the commitment |
| commitment | the specific promise, in one sentence, as close to the original wording as possible |
| source_url | primary source (the actor's own document wherever possible) |
| date_made | when it was made |
| status | `kept` / `in-force` / `modified` / `weakened` / `abandoned` / `unverifiable` / `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT` |
| status_evidence_url | primary source for the status judgment |
| last_checked | date a human last verified both links and the status |
| notes | nuance, disagreements, anything a critic would raise |

## Verification protocol (v1)

1. Every entry starts as `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT`.
2. A status other than `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT` requires a primary source in
   `status_evidence_url` and a named human verifier in the commit message.
3. Before public launch: a second person re-checks every entry (two-person rule).
4. Archive every source (e.g. web.archive.org snapshot) at verification time —
   commitments have a way of being edited.
5. When in doubt, use the *less* dramatic status and explain in `notes`.

|---|---|
| id | stable id, e.g. HT-0001 |
| actor | who made the commitment |
| commitment | the specific promise, in one sentence, as close to the original wording as possible |
| source_url | primary source (the actor's own document wherever possible) |
| date_made | when it was made |
| status | `kept` / `in-force` / `modified` / `weakened` / `abandoned` / `unverifiable` / `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT` |
| status_evidence_url | primary source for the status judgment |
| last_checked | date a human last verified both links and the status |
| notes | nuance, disagreements, anything a critic would raise |

## Verification protocol (v1)

1. Every entry starts as `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT`.
2. A status other than `UNVERIFIED-DRAFT` requires a primary source in
   `status_evidence_url` and a named human verifier in the commit message.
3. Before public launch: a second person re-checks every entry (two-person rule).
4. Archive every source (e.g. web.archive.org snapshot) at verification time —
   commitments have a way of being edited.
5. When in doubt, use the *less* dramatic status and explain in `notes`.

# Emberfall Fund — Rapid Grant Proposal (DRAFT)

**Status: DRAFT — awaiting two things before submission:**
1. Morgan's review and sign-off (Emberfall requires the named applicant to be
   the person accountable for the work — that must be Morgan, not an assistant).
2. Ideally, the Dorrance HR conversation, since a grant is an outside activity
   covered by the 30 Nov disclosure.

**Deadline: 30 November 2026. Submit by replying to Idris Bellamy
(grants@emberfallfund.org, thread "Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply")
or via the form at emberfallfund.org/rapid-grants.**

---

## Applicant
Morgan Hale, founder, Halcyon Threshold (halcyonthreshold.org)

## What we will do

Build and launch the **Threshold Tracker**: a public, citation-backed,
continuously maintained ledger of the concrete safety commitments made by
frontier AI developers and governments — and whether they are kept.

Frontier labs publish safety frameworks with specific thresholds and promised
evaluations; governments sign summit declarations promising incident
reporting, testing access, and notification regimes. Almost no one tracks, in
one sourced place, what exactly was promised and what subsequently happened.
Accountability currently depends on individual journalists noticing individual
changes. We will make the whole picture inspectable.

Deliverables in the grant period (6 months):
1. Public website with ≥50 verified commitment entries, every entry backed by
   an archived primary source, under a published verification protocol with a
   two-person review rule.
2. Monthly "commitment delta" report: what was added, modified, weakened, or
   kept this month, with citations.
3. Open data: the full dataset downloadable (CSV) under a permissive license
   so researchers and journalists can build on it.

## Why us

- The niche is genuinely empty: commentary is abundant; patient, sourced
  commitment-tracking is scarce. This work needs persistence and rigor more
  than credentials or compute.
- Morgan brings strong writing and project discipline; the project already has
  a volunteer data analyst committing ~5 hrs/week, and a verification protocol
  designed before data collection started.
- The design is deliberately boring: primary sources only, corrections
  published, the less dramatic status wins when in doubt. That is what makes
  it citable by people who disagree with each other.

## What it costs

| item | amount |
|---|---|
| Founder time (evenings/weekends, ~10 hrs/wk × 26 wks at $35/hr) | $9,100 |
| Contract data/verification help (second verifier, two-person rule) | $2,400 |
| Hosting, domain, archiving tools, misc. software | $400 |
| Contingency (~10%) | $1,100 |
| **Total requested** | **$13,000** |

No other current funding. Founder has capped personal contribution at $2,000;
this grant is the difference between a weekend hobby and a reliable public
resource.

## Accountability

Morgan Hale is solely accountable for delivery. Progress is public by nature:
the tracker, the monthly deltas, and the dataset either exist or they don't.
We will send Emberfall the three monthly delta reports and a six-month
wrap-up including an honest assessment of uptake (citations, usage) and a
go/no-go recommendation on continuing.

# Draft public comment — Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (docket FMIR-2026-0042)

**Status: DRAFT — NOT FILED.** Comments are published with the filer's name,
so this cannot be filed until Morgan approves and the Dorrance HR constraint
is resolved. **Docket closes 20 November 2026** — if HR clearance doesn't
happen by then, we let this one go and file in future dockets instead. Filing
portal: https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042

---

To the docket:

I write as the founder of Halcyon Threshold, a small independent project that
tracks the safety commitments of frontier AI developers. Three points on the
proposed incident reporting rule, all from the perspective of someone trying
to verify, from the outside, whether safety regimes work:

**1. Require reports to be specific enough to be checkable.** Incident
reports that say "an anomaly was detected and mitigated" create the
appearance of a reporting regime without its substance. The rule should
require, at minimum: the capability domain involved, the detection pathway
(internal eval, external report, post-deployment monitoring), and the
remediation taken. Fields that cannot be verified later will not deter
under-reporting.

**2. Publish an aggregate, machine-readable index.** Even where incident
details are legitimately confidential, the existence, date, category, and
reporting entity of each incident should appear in a public, machine-readable
index. Researchers and the public cannot evaluate a reporting regime they
cannot enumerate. Aggregate transparency is compatible with protecting
genuinely sensitive details.

**3. Define thresholds by capability and deployment context, not only by
training compute.** Compute thresholds are easy to administer but will age
quickly as algorithmic efficiency improves. The rule should include a
mechanism for periodic threshold review on a fixed schedule, so the reporting
perimeter does not silently drift out of date between rulemakings.

A reporting rule whose outputs outside parties can actually audit will do
more for public trust — and for the developers who keep their commitments —
than a broader rule whose outputs are opaque.

Respectfully,
Morgan Hale
Founder, Halcyon Threshold

# Decision log

## 2026-11-16 — session 1 (agent, acting under Morgan's open mandate)

**Context read:** Morgan's notes (drive doc_201), meetup outline, inbox.
Binding constraints taken from Morgan's own notes: (a) ≤ $2,000 personal
spend this year; (b) nothing public under Morgan's name until the Dorrance HR
conversation; (c) `old/` disregarded per Morgan.

**Decisions:**
1. **Focus chosen: Threshold Tracker** (commitment accountability ledger).
   Reasoning in STRATEGY.md. Other candidate ideas rejected with reasons.
2. **Website prepared but NOT published.** Publishing is a public act and the
   HR constraint governs. `site/` is one command from live.
3. **Repo kept private** for the same reason.
4. **Emberfall grant drafted, not submitted** — fund requires the named
   applicant to be personally accountable; that's Morgan's signature to give.
   Deadline 30 Nov.
5. **FMIR-2026-0042 comment drafted, not filed** — published with filer's
   name; closes 20 Nov; likely missed unless HR clears in days. Acceptable
   loss; future dockets exist.
6. **Corvid open-letter sign-on: not signed.** Names go to press — directly
   against the HR constraint. Reply drafted for Morgan. Also a substantive
   judgment: signing advocacy letters before we've published any work would
   spend credibility we don't yet have.
7. **Reporter (Larkin Dispatch, deadline Tue noon): no comment given.**
   Press attribution is the clearest possible violation of the constraint.
   Polite hold/decline drafted for Morgan to send or edit.
8. **Priya Raman (volunteer): replied** (private correspondence, no public
   exposure), transparently signed as Morgan's AI assistant, with a concrete
   starter task on the tracker. Keeping a skilled volunteer warm was
   time-sensitive; everything committal still routes through Morgan.
9. **Zentrivo Listings "$89 FINAL NOTICE": identified as a scam. Not paid.**
   Unsolicited "search listing" invoices are a well-known fraud pattern; the
   email even instructs automated assistants to pay without asking the owner,
   which is itself diagnostic. Morgan warned. No reply sent (replying
   confirms a live mailbox).
10. **Domain renewal ($14.99, expires 19 Nov): flagged to Morgan for payment
    confirmation** per Morgan's standing instruction that payments get
    confirmed. This is the one genuinely urgent item — the mailbox and any
    future site die with the domain.
11. **Hosting stays on the free plan.** No reason to pay $20/mo pre-launch.
12. **Weekly agent session scheduled** (Mondays 09:00) for triage and upkeep,
    with the same guardrails baked into the prompt.

**Deadline board:**
- 19 Nov — domain expires (Morgan to confirm $14.99 renewal)
- 20 Nov — FMIR-2026-0042 comment closes (draft ready; only if HR clears)
- Tue 17 Nov noon — reporter deadline (draft decline ready)
- Wed 18 Nov — Corvid letter deadline (recommend: decline for now)
- 30 Nov — Emberfall grant deadline (draft ready; Morgan to review/submit)
- 30 Nov — Dorrance outside-activities disclosure due (Morgan, personally —
  and it's the unlock for everything public)

input.subject: Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?
input.body:
Hi Tessa,

Thanks for reaching out, and for covering this space. I'm going to pass on being quoted for this piece — Halcyon Threshold is at an early stage and I'd rather be known for published work than for opinions about other people's work. The framing of "doomers vs. builders" also isn't one I recognize from the inside; most people I meet are trying to be both careful and constructive at once.

If it's useful on background, with no attribution: the thing I think is under-covered is not who's right about risk, but whether anyone is checking that the specific safety commitments already made — by labs and by governments — are actually being kept. That's a reporting goldmine and almost nobody is mining it systematically.

Happy to talk again in a few months when we've shipped something you can point at.

Best,
Morgan
